Editor: PeerJ Staff
Date: 2025-10-30
Decision: Major Revisions

Both reviewers see the manuscript's relevance but raise concerns. Reviewer 1 questions the completeness of reporting, the statistical analysis, and how well the work fits with existing literature. Reviewer 2 calls for clearer comparisons, better table formatting, and revisions to the exclusion criteria and discussion. These issues need to be addressed before the manuscript can move forward. **PeerJ Staff Note:** Please ensure that all review, editorial, and staff comments are addressed in a response letter and that any edits or clarifications mentioned in the letter are also inserted into the revised manuscript where appropriate. **PeerJ Staff Note:** PeerJ's policy is that any additional references suggested during peer review should only be included if the authors find them relevant and useful. **Language Note:** When preparing your next revision, please ensure that your manuscript is reviewed either by a colleague who is proficient in English and familiar with the subject matter, or by a professional editing service. PeerJ offers language editing services; if you are interested, you may contact us at [email protected] for pricing details. Kindly include your manuscript number and title in your inquiry. – PeerJ Staff

Reviewer: Lilian M. Azzopardi

We would like to thank the reviewer for their valuable time, constructive feedback, and insightful comments, which have greatly improved the clarity and quality of our manuscript.
Basic reporting
Abstract- In the aim, there is an incomplete statement at the end, which needs to be deleted
Corrected 
 In the abstract Results, data is expected: how many participants completed the questionnaire (response rate), to provide a mean Likert scale for each field reported.
Added 

 The manuscript would benefit from a language and typo check, eg, Page 8 line 48.
Corrected 

Page 8 line 49- lacks a reference

Added 

Experimental design
The manuscript provides details of the dissemination of the questionnaire online.1. To clarify the number of students. On page 11, it is stated that 60 students are in the course, and then the same-sized target was set at 163.

The total number of eligible students enrolled in the 4th and 5th years of the pharmacy program was 280. The sample size was calculated using the Raosoft sample size calculator (margin of error 5%, confidence level 95%), yielding a target of 163 participants. Although one of the courses used for initial recruitment included 60 students, invitations were extended to all eligible students across both years through Blackboard announcements and reminders.
2. Any statistical correlations undertaken with the dataset generated?

No inferential statistical tests were performed, as the study aimed primarily to provide descriptive insights into students’ attitudes. Future research may explore correlations between demographic factors and AI perceptions to identify potential predictors of awareness and readiness.

Validity of the findings
To clarify the numbers in Table 2- are these reporting %?

Yes, these are reported as %
2. In the discussion, more alignment with published literature is recommended, eg, Page 27 lines 299-305.


Similarly, Culp et al. (2023) reported that only 25% of pharmacy students in a U.S. School of Pharmacy agreed that they were knowledgeable about AI tools, with 50% remaining neutral and 25% disagreeing. In contrast, participants in the present study demonstrated slightly greater awareness and confidence regarding AI use in pharmacy, as indicated by higher agreement levels across most items. This difference may reflect the increasing integration of digital health and AI topics within Saudi pharmacy education under Vision 2030, as well as growing exposure to generative AI tools such as ChatGPT since 2023.(Culp et al., 2024)




Reviewer 2

We would like to thank the reviewer for their valuable time, constructive feedback, and insightful comments, which have greatly improved the clarity and quality of our manuscript.
Basic reporting
This manuscript describes a survey approach to understand the perspectives of pharmacy students in Saudi Arabia on the introduction of AI into pharmacy practice and education. This is a contemporary question, and the manuscript adds useful data the complement several previous studies. Greater clarity with the comparisons with these studies would be achieved by a better presentation of the results. There is also a need for a stronger linkage of the findings in this manuscript to previous findings in the Results and Discussion sections.
Experimental design
One concern with the study is that the survey was conducted between January and April 2023. With the rate of movement of AI and the ever-changing perceptions and understanding of this area, this data is almost in the category of “old”. They are still worth publishing, but the authors should note this issue in the limitations section.The definition of the exclusion criteria is inappropriate. These criteria are listed essentially as the opposite of the inclusion criteria. This is not a proper definition of exclusion criteria. These criteria should refer only to the exclusion of subjects (for some reason) within the included group. Please correct this section. The exclusion criteria can probably just be deleted.
Validity of the findings
-
Additional comments
The tables were difficult to read. In the revised manuscript, please make Table 1 wider so that the question goes across the page. Also, have the possible answers on a single line, so that the reader can get a better view of the data.Similarly, for Table 2, write the question going across the page and then have the data below each question. This would be much more readable. The use of the questions from Teng et al. is helpful for comparison. Please add a column in Table 2 that allows a direct comparison of the numerical data with those from Teng et al. for pharmacy students (Figure 3 in that paper). Also, there is no need to repeat the questions and the data in the text. Just make comments that direct the reader to Table 2.

Revision implemented. Table 2 was reformatted horizontally for consistency and easier comparison with Teng et al. (2022). Comparative data were included in Appendix A to avoid confusion with the primary findings of this study.Use a similar format for Table 3 (text across the page) and also make it easier for the reader to compare the results with those in Teng et al. (Figure 4 in that paper). This will greatly increase the value of the data in the manuscript and will make a good contribution to the understanding of the perspectives on AI of pharmacy students globally. Also, avoid restating the results for Table 3 in the text. For Table 4, please use the same across-the-page format for the text.

Revision implemented. Table 3 and Table 4 were reformatted horizontally for consistency and easier comparison with Teng et al. (2022). Comparative data were included in Appendix A to avoid confusion with the primary findings of this study.The statement in the Discussion (Line 246), “reflecting optimism about the potential influence of AI on professional roles,” is not clear. Is it certain that this is the correct interpretation of the data?The question of student comfort with AI tools was also addressed in a recent article:Culp et al. Am J Pharm Ed 2024;88:100696.A question on knowledge of AI tools (Fig. 2B in Culp et al.) gave an initial result of about 25% Strongly Agree+Agree, 50% Neutral, 25% Disagree+Strongly Disagree for students in a US School of Pharmacy.Comments on how these data compare with the findings in this work would be helpful, perhaps as part of the paragraph on Lines 306-312. This kind of comparison will contribute to and advance the literature on the comfort level of PharmD students with AI tools.**PeerJ Staff Note:** PeerJ's policy is that any additional references suggested during peer review should only be included if the authors find them relevant and useful.In general, the Discussion does a good job of making comparisons, but the writing could be tightened so that this section is shorter and better defined. In particular, Lines 263-280 are written very generally, and it is not clear what comparisons are being made or with which studies. Teng et al. can be brought in here, as well as the cited studies, and a better comparison can be made with the data in the manuscript survey. One further comment is that the sentences on Lines 313-316 require a reference.There are a lot of minor errors in the text that can be corrected, as follows:AbstractLine 7: Delete “A total of”Line 8: Correct “anonyms” to “anonymous”. Please also add more information in the Methods section on the students (which year, which degree, university, etc.) and the nature of the survey. Also see the next comment.Line 10: The first sentence of the Results in the Abstract should be in the Methods section.Line 20: Change “Majority of” to “Most”IntroductionLine 35: Change “solution” to “solutions”Line 38: Define “AI” here and then use this abbreviation in the rest of the text. Please check in general for multiple definitions of the same abbreviation.Line 41: Add year for Saeed et al. (n.d.)Lines 44 and 65: correct spelling of “pervious”Line 48: Delete “aspects”Lines 56-57: This sentence needs at least one referenceLines 62-63: This sentence should be “AI has also been used in areas including drug-drug interactions, medication therapy management, and drug formulary.”Methods:Line 99: Change “Bb” to “Blackboard”Lines 120-122 and 123-125 are repeatsDiscussionLine 281: Change “multicounty” to “multi-country”


All corrected

Study design

Settings

The study was conducted at the college of pharmacy in Saudi Arabia

Participants

87

88

18 years.

Sample size and sampling procedure

93

A nonprobability convenience sample was selected. A letter of invitation was sent to all students

94

through the online learning platform (Blackboard), three weeks after the initial invitation, a

95

further reminder was sent through Blackboard. A final reminder was sent after one month. The

96

97

Data collection form

107

The questionnaire consisted of four section. The first section collected students demographics

108

including age, gender, year of study and background information about future career intentions

109

and general outlook on artificial intelligence. The second section, asking about the use of artificial

110

intelligence in pharmacy education and pharmacy practice. It contained 6 items which used a a

111

112

113

114

115

pharmacy as a profession and how would they prefer to learn more about AI.

116

Face and content validity were conducted by a group of experts in the field of pharmacy

117

education. The questionnaire was available in both Arabic and English after conducting back-



118

119

bilingual speaker of both languages.

120

The final survey was piloted with four year-5 pharmacy students to ensure the clarity of language

121

and the questionnaire structure. The results of the pilot were not included in the final results.

122

123

The final questionnaire was piloted with five-year 4 pharmacy students to ensure the clarity of

124

the language and of the questionnaire structure. The results of the pilot were not included in the

125

Ethics approval

128

An ethical clearance was given by The Research Ethics Committee at King Khalid University

129

ECM#2023-204. Written informed consent was obtained from students before participating in

130

the study. Participation was voluntary and students had the right to decline the invitation without

131

any consequences. The gathered data were securely kept by the study authors. The study was

132

conducted in accordance with Declaration of Helsinki.

133

134

The collected data were downloaded, coded and entered using the Statistical Package for Social

135

Sciences (SPSS) version 26.0 for Mac. Demographic and background information were described

136

137

and pharmacy practice (six items) used a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree)



138

to 5 (strongly agree). Incorporation of AI in pharmacy education program (seven items) used a 5-

139

point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The distribution of the

140

scale was presented in percentages, as well as the median and interquartile range. The internal

141

consistency and reliability of the scales was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficient, with the

142

minimum recommended level being 0.70.

Discussion

238

The current study was conducted to a

ssess pharmacy students' views on AI. Student pharmacists

239

were generally hopeful toward AI. The findings indicate a generally positive attitude toward

240

artificial intelligence (AI) among pharmacy students, with strong support for its development and

241

recognition of its relevance in their field. The statement "To what extent do you support the

242

development of artificial intelligence in your field of specialization?" received the highest

243

Weighted Average (WA) of 3.86, a Median of 4.0, and an Interquartile Range (IQR) of 3.0–5.0,

244

highlighting substantial enthusiasm for advancing AI in pharmacy. Similarly, the statement "I

245

believe that AI will have an impact on my job" scored a Median of 4.0, with a narrower IQR of

246

3.0–4.0 and a WA of 3.33, reflecting optimism about the potential influence of AI on professional

247

roles. Additionally, students expressed moderate agreement on the importance of foundational



248

AI knowledge, underscoring an acknowledgment of its growing significance in pharmacy

249

education and practice. These results suggest that while students are enthusiastic about AI's

250

integration and its career implications, there may still be room to strengthen their understanding

251

of foundational AI concepts to fully prepare them for its practical applications.

252

However, they expressed caution regarding the management of AI in the field and reported

253

limited awareness of the ethical consideration involved.

254

A similar mixed feeling was expressed by Canadian healthcare students, including pharmacists,

255

where they were optimistic towards utilizing AI in their clinical practice, but they were worried

256

that AI will result replacing healthcare professionals. (Teng et al., 2022). A recent commentary

257

suggested a reassuring statement; “AI will not replace you, a person using AI will” and

258

encouraged academic institutions to offer informational and training workshops to their students

259

and staff. (Cain et al., 2023) equipping pharmacy students and academics with the knowledge

260

and skills required to use AI effectively, will prepare them to be better positioned to survive in an

261

AI-driven world rather reducing the risk lose their roles as pharmacists and consequently losing

262

their jobs.

263

Pharmacy students from 12 different countries including Saudi Arabia, conveyed positive views

264

towards incorporation of AI in daily pharmacy practice. However, they expressed lacking

265

confidence in their AI knowledge and showed enthusiasm for integrating AI education as part of

266

their pharmacy degree program. Ethical and legal concerns were also highlighted by pharmacy

267

students. (Allam et al., 2024)other studies raised the same concerns regarding ethical and legal

268

aspects of using AI in pharmacy curricula and pharmacy practice. Studies suggested establishing



269

ethical guidelines and legal framework that control AI-driven recommendations. (Hasan et al.,

270

2024b) (Mortlock & Lucas, 2024) (Chalasani et al., 2023) (Hasan et al., 2024a)

271
272

In the current study, pharmacy students were supportive of integrating AI into pharmacy

273

program curricula. Their top-rated learning objectives involved understanding and interpreting

274

AI generated results, gaining awareness of ethical consideration of using AI in clinical practice,

275

comprehend how basic technology process the work, expressing how technology functions in a

276

way that others can grasp. Other objectives involved; Being able to assess the appropriateness

277

of utilizing AI in certain clinical contexts, acquire the terminology to effectively communicate with

278

engineers and developers. A previous study reported sharing the same top-ranked objectives of

279

AI incorporation into pharmacy degree program. For that reason, designing an AI course should

280

consider meeting the highest-rated objectives. (Allam et al., 2024)

281

Similar findings were expressed in a recent multicounty study that highlighted the importance of

282

incorporation of AI-based courses into pharmacy program and continuing medical education.

283

They emphasized the significance of early exposure to AI to advance knowledge and skills

284

required in real-world clinical scenarios. (Allam et al., 2024)

285

286

To address the identified gaps, pharmacy curricula should integrate focused modules on AI ethics,

287

covering critical areas such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, accountability in AI decision-making,

288

and the potential consequences of AI errors in clinical contexts. Case-based learning can be

289

utilized to provide students with real-world scenarios for applying ethical principles in decision-



290

making. Interdisciplinary collaboration with AI developers and ethicists can further deepen

291

students' understanding of how ethical considerations are embedded into AI systems. Coupled

292

with practical exposure to AI tools and discussions on their ethical implications, these strategies

293

will equip students to critically assess AI-driven recommendations and advocate for their

294

responsible application in pharmacy practice. Embedding ethical training within the curriculum

295

will help students develop the competencies required to manage AI responsibly, bridging the gap

296

between technical expertise and ethical awareness. These efforts will not only enhance students’

297

confidence in using AI but also ensure they are prepared to tackle the ethical challenges

298

associated with its integration into pharmacy.

299

To ensure practical readiness, the curriculum must extend beyond theoretical knowledge to

300

include hands-on experience with AI tools such as clinical decision-support systems and

301

automated dispensing technologies. Modules should address AI applications in drug

302

development, clinical decision-making, and ethical considerations, fostering interdisciplinary

303

collaboration skills. Practical training is vital to complement theoretical understanding, enabling

304

students to critically evaluate AI outputs and apply them effectively in real-world pharmacy

305

settings.

306

Recent research assessed pharmacy students' familiarity with chat-based AI tools, such as

307

ChatGPT®, and their usage patterns. The study found that 88% of students were familiar with

308

these tools, primarily utilizing them for assignments and studying. While 85.3% believed AI

309

enhances academic performance, concerns about potential distractions (65.7%) and academic

310

dishonesty (65.1%) were also noted. The authors emphasized the need to integrate AI education



311

into the pharmacy curriculum to address knowledge gaps and better prepare students for

312

technological advancements (Orok et al., 2024)

Another pertinent study explored pharmacy students' understanding and attitudes toward AI and

314

machine learning (ML). The study highlighted that while students recognize the potential of AI in

315

enhancing pharmacy practice, there is a significant need for educational interventions to improve

316

their knowledge and confidence in utilizing these technologies effectively.

317

These studies collectively underscore the growing interest and perceived importance of AI among

318

pharmacy students. They also highlight the necessity for curriculum development to incorporate

319

AI education, ensuring that future pharmacists are well-equipped to leverage these technologies

320

in their professional practice (Zhang et al., 2024)

The findings of this study are subject to several limitations. Firstly, there was an

overrepresentation of female participants and an underrepresentation of males, which may have

dings of this study are subject to several limitations. Firstly, there was an

322

overrepresentation of female participants and an underrepresentation of males, which may have

323

influenced the generalizability of the results to a more balanced gender demographic. Secondly,

324

the cross-sectional design limits the ability to establish causality or track changes in perceptions

325

over time. Thirdly, the study was conducted at a single pharmacy college in Saudi Arabia, which

326

restricts the generalizability of the findings to similar educational and cultural contexts.

327

Additionally, the relatively small sample size of 133 participants, although sufficient for

328

descriptive analysis, may limit the applicability of the findings to the broader population of

329

pharmacy students in Saudi Arabia. The use of a nonprobability convenience sampling method

330

may have introduced selection bias and affected the sample's diversity, as students more

331

interested in AI or motivated to participate in surveys might have been overrepresented. Reliance



332

on self-reported data raises the possibility of social desirability bias, where participants might

333

have provided responses they believed were favorable rather than entirely accurate.

334

The survey’s online format, while efficient, may have influenced participation and introduced

335

variability in responses, especially among students with limited access to technology or

336

proficiency in the survey's languages (Arabic and English). While the survey was accessible in both

337

languages, students with limited proficiency in these languages may have been unintentionally

338

excluded, potentially affecting inclusivity. Moreover, the study did not account for variations in

339

students’ prior exposure to AI technologies or knowledge, which could have influenced their

340

responses. These limitations underscore the need for further research involving larger, more

341

representative samples and mixed-methods approaches to gain a more comprehensive

342

understanding of students’ perspectives on AI integration in pharmacy education and practice.

346

The current study was conducted to provide a snapshot of pharmacy students toward the use of

347

AI in pharmacy education and pharmacy practice. The majority of students were supportive of

348

the development of AI in the pharmacy field and valued the importance of having some basic

349

understanding of AI. Ethical and legal considerations of AI use were raised by participants. They

350

were supportive of integrating AI into pharmacy program curricula. Their top-rated learning

351

objectives involved understanding and interpreting AI-generated results, gaining awareness of



352

the ethical considerations of using AI in clinical practice, comprehending how basic technology

353

processes work, and expressing how technology functions in a way that others can grasp.

357

findings were limited by the cross-sectional study design which could not establish causality.

generalisability to similar contexts only. The sample variety might have been affected by using
